extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, screenwriters, playwrights, and filmmakers seeking practical scene-design and scene-analysis guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, writing, and analyzing dramatic scenes: creating emotions, mood, dilemmas/choices, subtext, beats, and locating turning points that make scenes turn and play. Geared especially to film/screenplay but applicable to prose and theatre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Diminishing Returns on repeated emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: A repeated presentation of the same serious emotion decreases its effect; repetition halves an emotion’s expected effect and repeated again can reverse the emotional charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid having scenes or beats that repeatedly demand the same intense emotional response from the audience. If you must repeat, create large contrasts so earlier events take on new meaning in retrospect. (McKee notes the humorous exception that sex may seem endlessly repeatable.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy structure: setup and punch; laughter is not an emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy consists of a setup that raises tension (often via taboo material) and a punch that releases it into laughter; laughter is a critical response, not a pure emotion, and may occur inside other emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write setups that build tension and time the punch so it hits when the setup is ripe; do not deliver punchlines nonstop—comic timing and sensitivity to audience fatigue matter. Example: bright light, full shots, and zany actors create a comic mood; change those elements and the same beats can feel threatening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast can permit apparent repetition without sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: If the contrast between successive events is so great that the earlier event is reinterpreted in light of the later one, a story can move positive-to-positive or negative-to-negative without sentimentality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design turns with sufficiently large valence contrast so the audience re-evaluates earlier moments (example: lovers argue then one kills the other — the earlier breakup may be read as positive given the later murder). Small-degree changes won’t produce this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish emotion (short-term) from feeling/mood (long-term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotion is a short-lived peak that burns rapidly; feeling (or mood in film) is a long-term background that colors days, personalities, and makes emotions specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what immediate emotion the scene must produce and what surrounding feeling/mood will make that emotion specific. Use mood to color and foreshadow but not to substitute for actual change in the scene’s arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mood must be created from textual/production qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mood in film/text is created by the sum of textural qualities: light/color, tempo of action and editing, casting, dialogue style, production design, and musical score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these elements consistently to foreshadow and shape audience anticipation; be aware mood influences specificity of emotion (comic vs thriller examples) but cannot replace dramatic turning or substantive scene change.

rubrics_metrics.name: The arc of a scene determines basic emotion; mood makes it specific
rubrics_metrics.description: What changes within the scene (its arc) determines whether the emotion is positive or negative; mood specifies which particular emotion the audience feels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus first on designing an arc that changes value; then layer mood to make the resulting emotion precise and textured. Don’t rely on mood photography to carry undramatized exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: True choice must be a dilemma (not obvious right/wrong)
rubrics_metrics.description: A turning-point choice is meaningful only when it is a dilemma — either between two irreconcilable goods or between the lesser of two evils. A choice between clear right and wrong is not a real choice dramatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pose choices that force the character to sacrifice or risk something of equal weight; avoid forced moral binaries which the audience can predict and which provide no dramatic tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid two-sided vacillation (positive/negative swing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-sided conflict that simply oscillates between positive and negative (e.g., 'she loves me/she loves me not') is repetitious, insoluble, and fails to provide true closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace simple vacillation with more complex relationships or dilemmas so the story can end decisively rather than leave the audience expecting the pattern to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular (three-sided) design for robust choice and closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a third corner (C) to an A vs B relationship to produce a triangle of relations; this multiplies relationship permutations, avoids repetition, and enables irreversible choices that close the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use three-sided conflicts to generate many variations (A/B/C positive/negative/neutral combinations, alliances, betrayals). When A chooses B over C (or vice versa), the sacrifice of C provides audience satisfaction and closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and layer text and subtext simultaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: Text is the sensory surface (what’s seen and heard). Subtext is the inner life—thoughts, feelings, unconscious impulses—hidden under the surface. Good scenes operate on both levels simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the observable actions and dialogue (text) and separately invent the characters’ unspoken objectives and impulses (subtext). Avoid writing dialogue that merely states inner truth ('on the nose').

rubrics_metrics.name: Make scenes 'actable' by providing an inner life for actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors create from subtext; if a scene has no inner life, it is 'unactable'—actors will smell the lie and refuse or invent subtext irrelevant to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave space for actors to realize subtext; if you force phony surface truth, actors will either reject it or substitute their own subtext, possibly undermining your intentions. Example: a candlelit 'I love you' scene needs an underlying motive (fear of loss, setting up a breakup, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats are the building blocks of a scene
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat is an exchange of action/reaction in character behavior, consisting of a textual action and the underlying subtextual action/reaction pairing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parse scenes into beats to see structure. Keep a beat as long as the action/reaction pair holds; start a new beat when behavior clearly changes. Beats aggregated create the scene arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name beats with active gerund phrases that capture subtext
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify each beat’s inner action with an emotive gerund (e.g., 'Begging', 'Groveling at her feet') and name reactions similarly (e.g., 'Ignoring the plea').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose phrasing that conveys feeling and intention, not literal activity. This helps reveal the emotional logic and makes it easier to see turning points and values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-step technique for scene analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical method to analyze scenes: (1) Define Conflict (who drives it, what they want, express desire as infinitive; identify antagonism), (2) Note Opening Value (positive/negative charge), (3) Break the Scene into Beats (name subtextual gerunds), (4) Note Closing Value and Compare (if unchanged, it's a nonevent), (5) Survey Beats and Locate Turning Point (find the moment expectation vs result opens a gap).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these steps to dissect why a scene plays or fails. The Turning Point is located by tracing action/reaction through beats to the moment that changes the scene’s end values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define conflict by phrasing desires as infinitives and ensure direct opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who drives the scene and state each side’s desire as an infinitive ('to do this', 'to get that'). A well-written scene will show that these desires are in direct conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also identify antagonistic forces (people, institutions, objects) and express their desires likewise. If desires are tangential rather than oppositional, the scene lacks clear conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opening vs closing value comparison to judge whether a scene turns
rubrics_metrics.description: Note the value charged at the scene’s opening (positive/negative) and at closing; if the two are identical, the scene is a nonevent (exposition, no turning). A changed value signals a turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit value notes when analyzing; this reveals whether the scene produced meaningful change or merely filled time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate the Turning Point as the moment when expectation and result diverge
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the arc of beats, the Turning Point is the precise moment the major gap opens between what the audience expects and what actually results, thereby changing end values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the gerund-labeled beats from opening to end; the Turning Point will appear as the pivotal beat where behavior or reaction breaks the pattern and redirects the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition-only scenes are boring: drama requires change
rubrics_metrics.description: Undramatized exposition—scenes that convey information without change—fails to create meaning regardless of mood or production values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing expository scenes that rely on mood to carry them; instead dramatize information through conflict, beats, and a turning point that alters value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use props, setting, minor characters to enrich subtext and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental details (e.g., vendor selling lace, lighting, camera angles, casting choices) can counterpoint or enrich the scene's emotional texture and imply subtext.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy such details to add connotative meaning (lace → weddings/sexuality, vendor → comic counterpoint) and to help actors and audience read subtext without explicit dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtext exists even in solitary narration and direct address
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration, soliloquy, or direct-to-camera address still contain subtext: characters may lie to themselves or dissemble even when 'confessing' to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write narrated 'confessions' with awareness of self-deception and hidden motives; subtext makes such moments rich rather than simply expository (examples: Annie Hall, voice-over).
